name: HTTP/3 and QUIC fingerprint
plain: QUIC's first packet carries a readable ClientHello, giving the same fingerprints as TLS plus transport parameters.
meaning: The QUIC Initial packet is encrypted with a public key, so middleboxes can read the TLS ClientHello and QUIC transport parameters. JA4 has a QUIC variant (prefix q). Connection ID length and version also differ per stack.

web.api: QUIC Initial packet decrypt at edge; JA4 q variant

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from the first packet of a fast connection
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your browser opens a new HTTP/3 connection
can: Compare the opening packet and its settings with known browsers
Use the same kind of fingerprint as normal secure connections
Spot scripts and bots with unusual connection details
cannot: Know your name or account from it
Tell two people on the same browser apart
Apply to sites that do not use HTTP/3

story.what_it_is: The first packet of the newest connection type shows readable clues about your browser.
story.for_you: You never see it. When your browser starts a fast new type of connection, the first message has readable details that match your browser and system. A server can tell real browsers from fake ones.
story.for_makers: Bot defense and fraud teams extend their older checks to the newest connection type. It gives them the same browser signature plus extra transport details. It also adds to a long term fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A bot defense reads the first packet and blocks tools that fake a browser name.
A game portal blocks cheat sellers that script account creation.
A retailer protects limited drops from bots.
A video site blocks scrapers that rip its streams.
An ad network filters click farms by connection pattern.
A researcher measures which browsers use the new connection type.

technical_bounds: ECH will hide inner ClientHello fields

history.change: RFC 9000 and 9001 define QUIC and its TLS binding
